items.explanation: Millions of young veterans became students on federal tuition money, swelling college campuses into major youth communities that would shape the decades that followed.
items.fact_source: u8.md §Key terms — GI Bill gave returning veterans college tuition and low-cost home loans, fueling suburbanization and the middle class

option_explanations.A: Correct. The GI Bill moved millions of young Americans onto college campuses, making campuses central places of youth life.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Unions remained strong in the postwar decades; the GI Bill is not connected to union decline.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Southern political shift followed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, not the GI Bill.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The GI Bill expanded federal support for education, and the Great Society later added federal aid to education.

options: (A) The growth of large college campuses as centers of youth life
(B) The decline of labor unions in American factories
(C) The movement of white Southerners from the Democratic Party into the Republican Party after 1964
(D) The end of federal aid to public education
items.stem: The GI Bill of 1944 sent millions of returning veterans to college on federal tuition benefits. This development contributed most directly to which of the following changes in American life?

items.explanation: 1968 combined a military shock (Tet), political assassinations, riots, and a chaotic convention — a concentration of upheaval that broke the postwar sense of shared national purpose.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — the Tet Offensive shattered public trust; assassinations, riots, and a chaotic Democratic convention made 1968 the year the postwar consensus died

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Major arms-control agreements belong to Nixon's détente policy of the 1970s, not 1968.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Tet Offensive, assassinations, riots, and the chaotic Democratic convention together made 1968 the year the postwar consensus died.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Those laws were passed in 1964 and 1965, not 1968.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The OPEC embargo was in 1973, five years later.

options: (A) The United States and the Soviet Union signed the first major Cold War arms-control agreements, opening the détente of the 1970s
(B) The Tet Offensive shattered public trust in the war, while assassinations, riots, and a chaotic convention shook the nation
(C) Congress passed the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act, completing the legislative goals of the civil rights movement
(D) The OPEC oil embargo forced Americans to confront the limits of cheap energy
items.stem: Historians often describe 1968 as "the year the postwar consensus died." Which of the following best supports that description?

items.explanation: Nixon was courting voters exhausted by the upheavals of the late 1960s — the riots, assassinations, and fractured movements — framing them as a quiet majority against a noisy minority.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — Richard Nixon courted the "silent majority"; 1968 assassinations, riots, and chaotic convention; the civil rights movement fractured

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Opposition to the Voting Rights Act was part of the Southern political shift, but Nixon's "silent majority" addressed a broader national unease with 1960s upheaval.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. GI Bill students belonged to an earlier postwar cohort; Nixon was appealing to those unsettled by the late 1960s, not to them.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The "silent majority" were Americans uneasy with the protests, riots, and cultural changes of the late 1960s.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Competition from Japanese imports is a late-1970s deindustrialization story, not the context of Nixon's 1969 appeal.

options: (A) Southern segregationists who opposed the Voting Rights Act of 1965
(B) College students who had benefited from the GI Bill's tuition payments and entered the workforce in the 1950s
(C) Americans who were uneasy with the protests, riots, and rapid cultural changes of the late 1960s
(D) Factory workers whose jobs were threatened by Japanese imports
items.stem: "And so tonight — to you, the great silent majority of my fellow Americans — I ask for your support." — Richard Nixon, address to the nation, November 3, 1969. Nixon's appeal to the "silent majority" was most directly aimed at which of the following groups?

stimulus.text: "And so tonight — to you, the great silent majority of my fellow Americans — I ask for your support." — Richard Nixon, address to the nation, November 3, 1969.

items.explanation: The civil rights movement's victories showed later movements how to organize — boycotts, marches, sit-ins, and direct pressure on Washington — and they adapted those strategies to their own causes.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — civil rights victories "opened doors for every movement that followed: women, Latinos, Native Americans, gay Americans, and people with disabilities all borrowed its strategies"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The school-integration argument was specific to the Black freedom struggle after Brown v. Board of Education.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Later movements borrowed the civil rights movement's strategies for organizing protest and pressing the federal government.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Segregationists opposed the civil rights movement; they were never its allies.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Southern voting rights were the specific goal of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, not the shared inheritance of the later movements.

options: (A) Its legal argument that the Fourteenth Amendment required school integration
(B) Its strategies for organizing protest and pressing demands on the federal government
(C) Its alliance with Southern white segregationists
(D) Its focus on winning voting rights for Black citizens in the segregated South through federal legislation
items.stem: After the mid-1960s, the women's movement, the Latino movement, the Native American movement, and the gay rights movement all drew on the civil rights movement's example. What did they most directly borrow from it?

items.explanation: The early movement won sweeping laws (1964, 1965), but afterward it split — over Black Power, the meaning of urban uprisings, and direction after King's 1968 assassination.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — "The movement later fractured — over Black Power, urban uprisings, King's 1968 assassination"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The 1964 and 1965 laws were sweeping but did not end racial inequality, and the movement continued.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. White Southerners moved toward the Republicans in reaction against the movement; electing Republicans was never the movement's goal.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The movement did not abandon racial justice goals.
option_explanations.D: Correct. After its legislative victories, the movement fractured over Black Power, urban uprisings, and King's 1968 assassination.

options: (A) The movement ended because the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 had fully solved racial inequality in America
(B) The movement shifted its focus to electing a Republican president
(C) The movement merged with the anti-war movement and abandoned racial justice goals
(D) The movement fractured over Black Power, urban uprisings, and responses to King's assassination
items.stem: Which of the following best describes the most important change in the civil rights movement after 1965?

items.explanation: The GI Bill moved millions of young veterans onto campuses, and the baby boom then supplied an even larger generation of students — making the campus the defining shared experience for a generation.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — the baby boom; §Key terms — GI Bill sent millions to college

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Redlining describes housing segregation; it says nothing about campus identity formation.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Highways shaped suburban and car-centered life, not campus identity.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The GI Bill plus the baby boom put an unprecedented share of young Americans on college campuses.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Strong unions describe workplace-centered life, which is the pattern the claim contrasts with campus life.

options: (A) Suburban homes were segregated by redlining and restrictive covenants
(B) The interstate highway system made long-distance car travel common for millions of suburban families across the nation
(C) The GI Bill sent millions of veterans to college, and the baby boom then filled campuses with youth
(D) Unions remained strong and factory wages supported a family
items.stem: A historian claims that the postwar decades produced the first American generation whose shared identity was formed more on college campuses than in workplaces or on farms. Which of the following provides the strongest evidence for this claim?

items.explanation: Federal education aid under the Great Society, following the GI Bill's earlier expansion, helped open schooling and college to the large baby-boom generation.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — Great Society: "Medicare, Medicaid, federal aid to education, immigration reform"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. School desegregation came from Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The baby boom was a demographic fact; education aid could not end it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Federal aid to education expanded schooling and college access for the growing youth population.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The GI Bill was not repealed.

options: (A) The desegregation of Southern public schools
(B) The end of the baby boom
(C) Expanded access to schooling and college for a growing youth population
(D) The repeal of the GI Bill and the end of federal tuition benefits for returning veterans
items.stem: The Great Society's program of federal aid to education contributed most directly to which of the following?

items.explanation: Carter was naming a mood built over a decade: Tet shattered trust in Vietnam, Watergate deepened distrust of the presidency, and stagflation broke faith in the government's economic toolkit.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — the Tet Offensive shattered public trust; Watergate deepened distrust of the presidency; stagflation "broke the Keynesian toolkit"; Carter's "crisis of confidence" speech (1979) named the mood

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The movement's victories did not produce such confidence; the mood Carter named was one of doubt.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The embargo exposed American vulnerability to foreign oil, not oil-company control of the government.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Lost trust over Vietnam, Watergate-era distrust, and stagflation together produced the crisis of confidence.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Young Americans of the era were highly politically active, from campuses to campaigns.

options: (A) The civil rights movement's legislative victories in 1964 and 1965 convinced Americans that the federal government could solve every social problem
(B) The OPEC embargo proved that American oil companies controlled the federal government
(C) The Vietnam War shattered public trust, Watergate deepened distrust of the presidency, and stagflation broke confidence in economic management
(D) The baby boom generation rejected all forms of political participation
items.stem: By 1979, Jimmy Carter told Americans the nation faced a "crisis of confidence." Which of the following best explains the origins of the mood he was describing?

items.explanation: Postwar prosperity was built on cheap energy — the interstate highways, the car, the suburban home. The embargo showed how exposed that way of life was to a cutoff of imported oil.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — "the OPEC oil embargo (1973)... exposed American vulnerability"; "the baby boom, the interstate highway system (1956), and cheap energy built a consumer society around the car and the single-family home"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Railroad regulation was a Gilded Age and Progressive Era issue, not a 1973 vulnerability.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. New Deal banking reforms dated to the 1930s; they were not what the embargo exposed.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The embargo exposed American dependence on cheap, imported energy for its car-centered suburban economy.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Agricultural exports were not the target or the lesson of the oil embargo.

options: (A) The federal government's inability to regulate the powerful railroad industry of the Gilded Age
(B) The failure of the New Deal's banking reforms
(C) The economy's dependence on cheap, imported energy to sustain its car-centered suburban life
(D) The collapse of American agricultural exports
items.stem: The OPEC oil embargo of 1973 exposed which of the following vulnerabilities in the postwar American economy?

items.explanation: The energy crisis and the televised hostage crisis fed a sense of national decline; conservatives argued the postwar bargain had failed, and Reagan's 1980 election closed the period.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — "a second energy crisis (1979)"; "the Iranian hostage crisis — 52 Americans held 444 days — televised it"; "By 1980 a growing conservative movement declared the postwar bargain a failure, and Reagan's election closed the period"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Civil Rights Act was passed in 1964, fifteen years earlier.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The crises of 1979 fed the conservative claim that the postwar bargain had failed, opening the way for Reagan.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Social Security was never repealed.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The League of Nations fight belonged to 1919, not 1979.

options: (A) The passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
(B) A growing conservative movement's claim that the postwar bargain had failed, opening the way for Reagan
(C) The repeal of the New Deal's Social Security program, ending federal old-age pensions and unemployment insurance
(D) The Senate's ratification of the League of Nations
items.stem: The second energy crisis of 1979, arriving alongside the Iranian hostage crisis, contributed most directly to which of the following political developments?

items.explanation: Postwar economic management assumed that inflation and unemployment moved in opposite directions. When both rose together, the standard policy tools could not fix one without worsening the other.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — "stagflation — inflation plus unemployment at once — broke the Keynesian toolkit"

option_explanations.A: Correct. Stagflation meant inflation and unemployment rose together, defeating the usual policy tradeoff.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Falling prices with full employment describes a healthy economy, the opposite of stagflation.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Rapid growth with balanced budgets is prosperity, not stagflation.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Tariffs and closed markets describe trade policy, not the inflation-unemployment combination.

options: (A) Rising inflation and rising unemployment at the same time
(B) Falling prices and full employment
(C) Rapid economic growth with balanced federal budgets and full employment
(D) High tariffs and closed markets
items.stem: Stagflation in the 1970s "broke the Keynesian toolkit" because it combined which of the following?

items.explanation: The highways, cheap gasoline, and suburban homes formed one system: Americans drove everywhere because the built environment gave them no alternative, which made any oil cutoff painful.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — "the interstate highway system (1956), and cheap energy built a consumer society around the car and the single-family home"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The highways promoted gasoline-powered cars, not electric trains.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The highway system locked in car-dependent suburban life built on cheap gasoline.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Sun Belt boomed while inner cities decayed — people moved outward, not back into cities.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The American economy remained deeply tied to world trade, including imported oil.

options: (A) Replacing the railroad network with a national system of electric trains
(B) Encouraging a car-dependent suburban life built on cheap gasoline
(C) Forcing Americans to abandon the suburbs and move back into crowded inner cities
(D) Ending American dependence on foreign trade
items.stem: The interstate highway system, begun in 1956, contributed to the energy vulnerability of the 1970s by...

items.explanation: The 1970s oil shocks showed that the abundance Americans took for granted — cheap gasoline, endless driving, energy-hungry suburbs — depended on imported energy that could be cut off.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — the OPEC embargo (1973) and the second energy crisis (1979) "exposed American vulnerability"; Carter's "crisis of confidence" speech (1979)

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The GI Bill describes educational expansion in the 1940s, not resource limits in the 1970s.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Civil rights legislation addressed racial inequality, not the limits of natural resources.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The oil shocks exposed how dependent American prosperity was on cheap, imported energy.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The baby boom increased the population, but population growth alone does not show an era of limits.

options: (A) The GI Bill sent millions of veterans to college
(B) The Civil Rights Act outlawed segregation in public places
(C) The OPEC embargo and the second energy crisis exposed American dependence on cheap, imported energy
(D) The baby boom increased the American population, straining schools, housing, and public services across the nation
items.stem: An environmental historian argues that the 1970s marked a turning point from an era of assumed abundance to an era of limits. Which of the following provides the strongest support for this interpretation?

items.explanation: Carter spoke in the summer of 1979, with gasoline lines fresh in memory and 52 Americans held hostage in Iran — the twin crises that made decline feel real to many Americans.
items.fact_source: u8.md §The story — "a second energy crisis (1979)"; "Carter's 'crisis of confidence' speech (1979) named the mood, and the Iranian hostage crisis — 52 Americans held 444 days — televised it"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Tet Offensive and the Tonkin Resolution belonged to the Vietnam escalation of the 1960s.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The League of Nations debate belonged to 1919.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Panic of 1893 belonged to the 1890s depression.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The speech came amid the second energy crisis and the Iranian hostage crisis.

options: (A) The Tet Offensive during the Vietnam War and the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution authorizing escalation
(B) The Senate debate over the League of Nations
(C) The Panic of 1893 and the depression that followed
(D) A second energy crisis and the Iranian hostage crisis, which fed a sense of national decline
items.stem: Carter's 1979 "crisis of confidence" speech was delivered in the context of which of the following?

items.explanation: The League fight was the classic American argument: should the nation commit itself to shaping world affairs through international organizations, or stay out of foreign entanglements? The Senate chose to stay out, and the country turned inward.
items.fact_source: u7.md §The story — "Wilson's dream of a League of Nations died in the Senate, and the country turned inward"

option_explanations.A: Correct. The League debate was the isolationism-versus-internationalism argument in its classic form.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The silver-versus-gold debate belonged to the 1890s money question.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Federalist/Anti-Federalist debate belonged to the 1780s.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Railroad regulation was a domestic Progressive issue, not the League question.

options: (A) The debate between isolationism and internationalism — whether America should entangle itself in world affairs
(B) The debate between free silver and the gold standard
(C) The debate between the Federalists and the Anti-Federalists over ratifying the Constitution in the 1780s, which shaped the early republic
(D) The debate over whether the federal government should regulate railroads
items.stem: The Senate's rejection of the League of Nations is best understood as an expression of which of the following recurring debates in American history?

items.explanation: The poster shows the federal government mobilizing the entire population for a European war in 1917. Just a few years later, the Senate rejected the League of Nations and the country turned inward — the sharp contrast is the point.
items.fact_source: u7.md §The story — the United States entered World War I in April 1917; "Wilson's dream of a League of Nations died in the Senate, and the country turned inward"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Senate rejected League membership; the United States never joined.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Congress never declared war on Germany a second time.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Red Scare of 1919–1920 followed the war; the poster campaign did not end it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Mass mobilization for Wilson's war was followed by rejection of his League and an inward turn.

options: (A) The mobilization continued into the 1920s through American membership in the League of Nations
(B) The poster campaign convinced Congress to declare war on Germany a second time in 1921, renewing the draft and the Liberty Bond drives
(C) Wartime mobilization ended the Red Scare of 1919–1920
(D) The country that mobilized so completely for Wilson's war then rejected his League of Nations and turned inward

items.explanation: Monroe had warned Europe to stay out of the Americas. Roosevelt kept the doctrine's name but reversed its direction: now the United States claimed the right to intervene in Latin America itself.
items.fact_source: u7.md §Key terms — Roosevelt Corollary (1904): "claimed a U.S. right to intervene in Latin America to keep European powers out, extending the Monroe Doctrine"; §The story

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The corollary extended the Monroe Doctrine; it did not repeal it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The corollary converted Monroe's warning to Europe into a license for American intervention in Latin America.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The corollary concerned Latin America and the Western Hemisphere, not Asia.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The corollary was a presidential policy statement, not a Senate-ratified treaty.

options: (A) It repealed the Monroe Doctrine entirely and withdrew the United States from all political and military involvement in the Western Hemisphere
(B) It turned a warning against European intervention into a justification for American intervention in Latin America
(C) It applied the Monroe Doctrine to Asia for the first time
(D) It made the Monroe Doctrine a formal treaty ratified by the Senate
items.stem: "Roosevelt... claimed, in his corollary to the Monroe Doctrine, an American right to police the hemisphere." The Roosevelt Corollary changed the meaning of the Monroe Doctrine in which of the following ways?

stimulus.text: Roosevelt "claimed, in his corollary to the Monroe Doctrine, an American right to police the hemisphere."

items.explanation: The Neutrality Acts were meant to keep America out of another war, but escalating economic pressure on Japan led step by step to Pearl Harbor — neutrality on paper, drift toward war in practice.
items.fact_source: u7.md §What the exam tests here — "WWII entry came through Pearl Harbor after escalating embargoes showed the Neutrality Acts had failed"

option_explanations.A: Correct. Escalating embargoes drew the United States toward war with Japan despite the neutrality laws, ending at Pearl Harbor.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Great Depression began with the 1929 crash, before the Neutrality Acts existed.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Schenck v. United States (1919) concerned the Espionage Act's crackdown on dissent, not neutrality legislation.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The United States helped found the United Nations after World War II.

options: (A) Despite neutrality laws, the United States drifted toward war with Japan, culminating in Pearl Harbor
(B) The Neutrality Acts caused the Great Depression by cutting off nearly all American trade with Europe and Asia
(C) The Neutrality Acts were repealed by the Supreme Court in Schenck v. United States
(D) The Neutrality Acts prevented the United States from joining the United Nations
items.stem: The review notes that "escalating embargoes showed the Neutrality Acts had failed." Which of the following best explains this judgment?

items.explanation: The war left America holding the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico, and the central argument was philosophical: could a republic built on self-government justify ruling other peoples?
items.fact_source: u7.md §The story — the Spanish-American War "ignited debate over whether a republic should rule colonies"; §What the exam tests here — "know the arguments for and against imperialism after the Spanish-American War"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Statehood for the Philippines was not the central question of the debate.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The debate centered on whether a republic founded on self-government should rule overseas colonies.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Monroe Doctrine concerned the Americas, not the Pacific empire question.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The League of Nations debate came two decades later, after World War I.

options: (A) Whether the Philippines should be admitted as a state immediately
(B) Whether a republic founded on self-government should rule overseas colonies
(C) Whether the Monroe Doctrine applied to the Pacific Ocean
(D) Whether the United States should join the League of Nations after the end of the First World War
items.stem: After the Spanish-American War of 1898 left the United States holding the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico, American debate over imperialism centered on which of the following questions?

items.explanation: Wilson had kept the country neutral, but unrestricted submarine attacks on shipping and Germany's secret proposal of a Mexican alliance against the United States made neutrality untenable.
items.fact_source: u7.md §The story — "Wilson kept the country neutral until German submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram pushed him to ask Congress for war in April 1917"; §What the exam tests here — WWI entry rested on submarine warfare, the Zimmermann telegram, and economic ties to the Allies

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Pearl Harbor was the cause of American entry into World War II, in 1941.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Soviet Union's control of Eastern Europe belonged to the Cold War, decades later.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram's secret alliance offer pushed Wilson to ask for war in April 1917.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The League of Nations was created after the war; it could not have caused American entry.

options: (A) The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, which brought the United States into the Second World War
(B) The Soviet invasion of Eastern Europe
(C) German submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram's secret offer of a German-Mexican alliance
(D) The collapse of the League of Nations
items.stem: Which of the following most directly pushed Wilson to ask Congress for war against Germany in April 1917?

items.explanation: The Senate's League rejection, the 1920s immigration quotas, and the Red Scare all point toward withdrawal — but a truly isolationist nation would not keep ruling the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico. The empire is the strongest counter-evidence.
items.fact_source: u7.md §The story — the 1898 empire: "holding the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico"; the Senate rejected League membership and "the country turned inward"; immigration quotas of 1921 and 1924

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Senate's rejection of the League supports the isolationist description; it does not challenge it.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The immigration quotas were part of the inward, nativist turn; they support the description.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Continuing to rule an overseas empire contradicts the claim of pure isolationism.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Red Scare was part of the postwar inward panic; it supports the description.

options: (A) The Senate rejected membership in the League of Nations, refusing any American commitment to collective security
(B) Congress passed immigration quotas aimed at southern and eastern Europeans and Asians
(C) The United States continued to hold the Philippines, Guam, and Puerto Rico, the overseas empire won in 1898
(D) The Red Scare of 1919–1920 targeted suspected communists and anarchists
items.stem: A historian describes the United States of the 1920s as purely isolationist. Which of the following presents the strongest challenge to that description?

items.explanation: American banks lent heavily to Britain and France and American factories sold them war goods. Those ties meant the United States was never a disinterested bystander, and they pulled American policy toward the Allies.
items.fact_source: u7.md §What the exam tests here — "WWI entry rested on submarine warfare, the Zimmermann telegram, and economic ties to the Allies"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The United States traded heavily with Europe; it was not cut off from European commerce.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Extensive American trade and loans with Britain and France made genuine neutrality difficult to sustain.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. American economic ties were to the Allies, not to Germany.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Allies did not pay the United States to enter the war.

options: (A) The United States had no trade with any European country before 1917
(B) Extensive American trade and loans with Britain and France made genuine neutrality difficult to sustain
(C) Germany was America's largest trading partner, and the United States wanted to protect that profitable trade
(D) The Allies paid the United States to enter the war
items.stem: In explaining why the United States entered World War I, historians cite German submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram — and also American economic ties to the Allies. Those economic ties mattered because...

items.explanation: Cut off from British goods first by Jefferson's embargo and then by war, Americans built their own factories — and having survived a second war with Britain, they felt a new national pride. Industry and nationalism grew together.
items.fact_source: u4.md §The story — "his 1807 Embargo Act, meant to punish Britain and France, cut Americans off from British manufactured goods and forced them to make their own. The War of 1812 did the same thing more dramatically. When the war ended, a wave of national pride and new factories produced what Americans called the Market Revolution"

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The United States did not conquer Canada in the War of 1812.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The war accelerated the Market Revolution; it did not end it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Trade with Britain resumed after the war.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The cutoff from British goods forced domestic manufacturing, and surviving the war fed national pride.

options: (A) The United States decisively conquered Canada and seized British colonies
(B) The war ended the Market Revolution and restored subsistence farming as the foundation of the entire American economy for decades
(C) Britain agreed to abandon all trade with the United States permanently
(D) Cut off from British goods, Americans built their own factories — and surviving a second war with Britain fed national pride
items.stem: The War of 1812 ended in stalemate, yet it fueled American nationalism and domestic industry. Which of the following best explains why a stalemated war had these effects?

items.explanation: The print shows an official, large-scale public celebration — evidence that contemporaries saw the canal as a proud collective achievement, the kind of internal improvement that tied the young nation together.
items.fact_source: u4.md §The story — canals like the Erie (1825) "tied distant regions into one commercial web"; §Key terms — Erie Canal: "Waterway linking the Great Lakes to New York City; made New York the commercial capital"

option_explanations.A: Correct. The official celebration shows Americans treating the canal as a proud national achievement that tied the country together.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The canal served American commerce; British merchants did not control it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The canal made New York the commercial capital; New Yorkers celebrated it rather than opposing it.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Canal-building continued as part of the Market Revolution; the celebration did not mark its end.

options: (A) Americans treated internal improvements like the canal as proud national achievements that tied the country together
(B) The canal was celebrated mainly by British merchants who controlled American trade
(C) New Yorkers opposed the canal because it threatened the city's commerce
(D) The celebration marked the end of all canal-building in the United States, since railroads had already replaced water transport

option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Louisiana Purchase, not the Embargo Act, was the treaty with France.

options: (A) A successful use of economic pressure that forced Britain to change its policies toward American trade

items.explanation: The act's own language shows the mechanism: reservations would be surveyed and divided into individual allotments, and the leftover 'surplus' would be sold — moving land from Native nations to white settlers.

option_explanations.B: Correct. Allotment divided reservations into individual parcels, and the unallotted 'surplus' was sold to white settlers.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The act opened reservation land to white settlement; it did not protect it.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Allotment broke up common tribal holding into individual parcels; it did not restore it.

options: (A) Purchasing all reservation land at fair market value
(B) Dividing reservations into allotments and selling the 'surplus' land to white settlers
(C) Granting reservations permanent protection from white settlement and federal interference
(D) Returning reservation land to tribal ownership in common

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Promising to shrink the agency is opposition, not support.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The backlash position — regulation threatens jobs and freedom — had become presidential policy.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The EPA still existed; Reagan promised to shrink it.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The laws remained on the books; the fight was over enforcement and scope.

items.stem: Carson documented that DDT was poisoning ecosystems — and readers. Why did the "and readers" part of her finding matter so much?
options: (A) It proved only farmers were ever affected by pesticides
(B) It showed readers were causing the pollution themselves
(C) It made pollution a human-health issue for a wider audience
(D) It limited the book's appeal to professional scientists
items.explanation: A book about birds alone might have stayed a nature book; showing that readers themselves were being poisoned made it everyone's issue.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The point was that exposure reached ordinary readers, not just farm workers.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Carson blamed the chemical industry and complacency, not individual readers.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Human-health stakes converted a nature concern into a mass concern.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The health angle broadened the audience; it did not narrow it.

items.stem: The great environmental statutes cluster in 1970–73: the EPA and Clean Air Act in 1970, Clean Water in 1972, Endangered Species in 1973. Why did they come in this burst?
options: (A) The president personally ordered Congress to pass the laws on a fixed schedule
(B) Industry lobbyists wrote the laws and pushed them through Congress
(C) The Supreme Court required Congress to act on pollution
(D) Earth Day and visible disasters created pressure Congress could not ignore
items.explanation: Twenty million people on Earth Day plus oil-coated beaches and a burning river gave Congress both the motive and the political cover to legislate quickly.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Congress responded to public pressure; no presidential timetable drove the burst.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Industry generally resisted the new regulations; it did not author them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. No court order produced these statutes.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Mass mobilization plus visible crisis is what concentrates legislative action.

(C) The government had solved industrial pollution by 1978
(D) Toxic waste was only ever a problem in rural areas
items.explanation: Love Canal put pollution inside people's houses and schoolyards, making the threat personal in a way distant spills had not.

option_explanations.A: Correct. A residential neighborhood on top of toxic waste made the danger hit home — literally.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The issue was buried chemical waste under homes, not canal water supply.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The scandal showed pollution problems were unresolved.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Love Canal was a suburban neighborhood, not a rural area.

(C) It showed that pollution affected only the state of Ohio
(D) It was staged by activists purely for the cameras

option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The river's power as a symbol was national, not confined to Ohio.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The fires were real consequences of industrial waste, not staged events.

(C) Pollution in the United States had ended for good
(D) The new agency replaced Congress as the lawmaker on pollution

option_explanations.B: Incorrect. States kept their own environmental authority; the EPA added a federal layer.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The agency was created to fight ongoing pollution, not to mark its end.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Agencies enforce laws; Congress still writes them.

items.stem: The Santa Barbara spill came in 1969, the first Earth Day in 1970, and the major statutes in 1970–73. What does this sequence show about how the movement worked?

(C) Legislation came first and the disasters followed afterward

option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The sequence runs the other way: disaster, then mobilization, then law.

option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The industry survived; its reputation for automatic beneficence did not.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The book belongs to the decade's broader questioning of established authority.

items.stem: A historian argues the environmental movement succeeded because it copied the civil rights movement exactly. What is the best evaluation of this argument?

(B) The movements shared a toolkit, but "exactly" overstates it
(C) The two movements had nothing in common
(D) Environmentalism came before the civil rights movement began
items.explanation: The review supports the shared-tools parallel but not identity: borrowing a political method is not the same as copying a movement, and the opponents — segregationists versus industry and anti-regulation conservatives — were different.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. "Exactly" claims too much; the parallel the review draws is about tools, not identity.
option_explanations.B: Correct. It accepts the documented parallel while rejecting the overstatement.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The review explicitly draws the parallel on tools and on the backlash wall.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The civil rights movement's major victories came in the 1960s, before the environmental statutes of the 1970s.

items.stem: The photograph shows American delegates — including Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes — leaving a session of the Washington Naval Conference in 1921. What does American leadership of this disarmament conference show about 1920s foreign policy?

stimulus.image_caption: American delegates, including Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes, leaving D.A.R. Hall during the Washington Naval Conference, September 1921 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1921 U.S. government photograph published before 1930; Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) The United States had joined the League of Nations
(B) The United States refused to negotiate with any of the other great powers
(C) The U.S. would limit war's costs but accept no binding commitments
(D) The conference produced a binding military alliance among its members
items.explanation: The review presents Washington as the paradigm of 1920s policy: serious disarmament diplomacy with real savings, but no enforcement mechanism and no entangling commitments.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Senate had rejected League membership; the conference was outside the League.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Convening and leading the conference was active diplomacy, not refusal to negotiate.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Leading on disarmament while accepting no binding commitments is the review's definition of the era's approach.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The treaties limited ships and pledged principles; they created no alliance.

items.stem: This American battleship, the USS Washington, was still under construction when it was sunk as a gunnery target in 1924. Why was an unfinished American battleship destroyed?

stimulus.image_caption: The battleship USS Washington (BB-47) being sunk as a target, 1924 (U.S. Navy photograph).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1924 U.S. Navy photograph; work of the U.S. federal government, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) It was sunk during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor
(B) The Navy had decided that battleships were now useless
(C) Congress cancelled it after the Depression began
(D) Treaty terms required scrapping ships under construction
items.explanation: Hughes stunned the conference by offering to scrap American ships already being built if others did the same; the treaty then required the scrapping, and the unfinished Washington was sunk as a target.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Pearl Harbor came in 1941; the Washington was sunk in 1924.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Navy still valued battleships; the scrapping was a treaty obligation, not a judgment on the ship type.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The sinking was in 1924, five years before the Depression began.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The ship was a casualty of the disarmament bargain Hughes proposed.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Washington Naval Conference (1921–22) — Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes stunned delegates by proposing the United States scrap ships already under construction if others did the same

items.stem: The photograph shows the Japanese delegation with Secretary Hughes at the Washington Conference. Japan accepted the treaty's 5:5:3 ratio but renounced the naval limits in the mid-1930s, then built the fleet that struck Pearl Harbor. What best explains Japan's turn against the treaty?

stimulus.image_caption: The Japanese delegation — with Secretary of State Hughes — at the Washington Naval Conference, 1921 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1921 photograph published before 1930; Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Japan resented its inferior 5:3 ratio as a racial insult
(B) Japan was genuinely pleased with the naval ratio it had received
(C) The treaty gave Japan more capital ships than Britain did
(D) Japan had never signed the naval limitation treaty at all
items.explanation: The review identifies the resentment directly: Japan read its assigned inferiority as a racial insult, which is why it walked away from the limits in the mid-1930s.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The perceived insult of the inferior ratio drove Japan to renounce the limits.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Japan protested the ratio; it did not welcome it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The ratio gave Britain and the U.S. five ships for Japan's three.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Japan signed, then renounced the limits in the mid-1930s.

items.stem: A student claims the Five-Power Treaty's capital-ship ratios of 5:5:3:1.75:1.75 treated all five signatories as equals. What is the best evaluation of this claim?
options: (A) The ratios locked in Anglo-American superiority over Japan
(B) The student's claim is correct, and all five of the navies were made equal
(C) The ratios applied only to the French and Italian navies
(D) The ratios were merely proposed but never written into the actual treaty
items.explanation: The numbers themselves refute the claim: five for the U.S. and Britain, three for Japan, and 1.75 each for France and Italy is a hierarchy, not equality.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Reading the numbers shows a ranked order with Japan deliberately placed below the Anglo-American powers.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The ratios are visibly unequal; that inequality was the point.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The ratios covered all five powers, including the U.S. and Britain.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The ratios were the treaty's core provision.

items.stem: Alongside the naval ratios, the Washington Conference produced a Four-Power Treaty pledging respect for Pacific island possessions and a Nine-Power Treaty pledging the Open Door in China. What did this combination show about American aims?
options: (A) The United States annexed new Pacific islands
(B) The United States closed China to all foreign trade
(C) The U.S. wanted Asian stability without binding commitments
(D) The treaties created an American-led Asian military alliance
items.explanation: Respecting possessions and the Open Door were principles, not commitments: Washington sought a stable Asia through pledges rather than through alliances or enforcement.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Four-Power Treaty pledged respect for existing possessions; it annexed nothing.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Nine-Power Treaty pledged the Open Door — keeping China open, not closing it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Principles without enforcement is the conference's signature approach.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. No alliance was created; the treaties deliberately avoided binding commitments.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Washington Naval Conference (1921–22) — companion treaties pledged respect for Pacific island possessions (Four-Power) and the Open Door in China (Nine-Power)

items.stem: The photograph shows the signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact at the Quai d'Orsay in Paris on August 27, 1928. Eventually 62 nations renounced war "as an instrument of national policy." What did the pact require signatories to do if a nation broke the pledge?

stimulus.image_caption: The signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact at the Quai d'Orsay, Paris, August 27, 1928 (French press photograph).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1928 French press photograph published before 1930; Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Send troops against the aggressor
(B) Pay reparations to the victim
(C) Nothing — the pact had no enforcement mechanism
(D) Expel the aggressor from the League of Nations entirely
items.explanation: The ceremony was grand and the promise sweeping, but the pact created no enforcement, no definition of aggression, and a wide self-defense loophole — so a violation triggered nothing.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The pact authorized no military action against violators.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. It provided for no reparations or penalties.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The absence of enforcement is the review's central point about the pact.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The pact had no expulsion procedure, and the United States was not in the League in any case.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) — a sweeping pact in which eventually 62 nations renounced war "as an instrument of national policy"; the pact had no enforcement mechanism, no definition of aggression, and a self-defense loophole

items.stem: Secretary of State Frank Kellogg, shown here, privately called the pact that bears his name nearly worthless. What does that private judgment show?

stimulus.image_caption: Frank Billings Kellogg, Secretary of State, in an official portrait (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Official portrait, Library of Congress; published before 1930, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Kellogg personally opposed the cause of peace
(B) The pact's own architect doubted paper promises could stop war
(C) The pact was never actually signed in Paris
(D) France wrote the pact entirely without any American involvement
items.explanation: Kellogg's private dismissal reveals the gap between the decade's public idealism and what its own diplomats believed: a treaty without enforcement was a gesture, not a guarantee.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Kellogg negotiated the pact; his doubt was about its effectiveness, not about peace.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The architect's own verdict exposes the wishful thinking behind the era's paper treaties.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The pact was signed in Paris in August 1928 by many nations.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The pact grew from a French proposal through Kellogg's own diplomacy.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) — Kellogg himself privately called it nearly worthless

items.stem: Within three years of the Kellogg-Briand signing, Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) in open violation of the pact and suffered no real consequence. What does this episode show?
options: (A) The pact caused the invasion of Manchuria
(B) The League of Nations punished Japan severely
(C) The Kellogg-Briand Pact prevented further invasions in the 1930s
(D) Unenforced treaties cannot bind a power determined to break them
items.explanation: Manchuria is the review's test case: an open violation with no consequence proved the pact — and the wishful thinking behind it — could not restrain aggression.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Japan invaded for its own imperial reasons; the pact did not cause the invasion.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Japan suffered no real consequence, which is precisely the point.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Italy, Germany, and Japan all committed aggressions in the 1930s despite the pact.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The episode is the clearest demonstration of the pact's toothlessness.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) — within three years Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) in open violation and suffered no real consequence

items.stem: This 1933 portrait shows Franklin Roosevelt in his first year as president. In his 1933 inaugural address he pledged the United States would be a "good neighbor" rather than a policeman in Latin America. What changed from the Roosevelt Corollary era?

stimulus.image_caption: Franklin Delano Roosevelt, official portrait, 1933 (White House).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1933 official White House portrait; work of the U.S. federal government, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) From strict isolationism to a new overseas empire
(B) From a claimed right to intervene to renouncing armed intervention
(C) Nothing changed in actual practice
(D) From non-intervention to new military occupations across the region
items.explanation: The Roosevelt Corollary had claimed a right to intervene; the Good Neighbor Policy renounced armed intervention — the review calls it a direct repudiation, same hemisphere, opposite method.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The shift was away from intervention, not toward empire.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The doctrine reversed: intervention claimed in 1904 was renounced in the 1930s.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The occupations of Haiti and elsewhere were wound down and the Montevideo convention renounced intervention.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The occupations ended; no new ones began.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Good Neighbor Policy (1930s) — announcing the Good Neighbor Policy in his 1933 inaugural address, FDR pledged the U.S. would be a "good neighbor" rather than a policeman; the direct repudiation of the Roosevelt Corollary

items.stem: Hoover withdrew Marines from Nicaragua, and Roosevelt signed the 1933 Montevideo convention renouncing armed intervention. Why did non-intervention become American policy in the 1930s?
options: (A) Latin American governments demanded still more American military interventions
(B) The Roosevelt Corollary legally required the withdrawal
(C) Depression-era costs ended intervention; Washington wanted markets and cooperation
(D) Congress abolished the State Department entirely
items.explanation: The review gives a two-part cause: principle plus economics — scarcity at home made intervention unaffordable, and Washington valued trade and future cooperation over the resentment occupations produced.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Latin America resented the interventions; it did not request more.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Corollary claimed a right to intervene; the Good Neighbor repudiated it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Depression-era scarcity plus the desire for markets and cooperation drove the reversal.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The State Department continued; the policy changed, not the institution.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Good Neighbor Policy (1930s) — the policy was partly principle and partly economics: the Depression made foreign adventures expensive, and Washington wanted Latin American markets and wartime cooperation, not resentment

items.stem: This is Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes, the central American figure at the Washington Naval Conference. Why does the review make Hughes, rather than President Harding, the main actor in the disarmament story?

stimulus.image_caption: Charles Evans Hughes, Secretary of State, in an official portrait (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Official portrait, Library of Congress; published before 1930, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Hughes conceived and drove the disarmament diplomacy
(B) Harding publicly opposed holding the conference
(C) The Constitution gives the Secretary of State sole power to make treaties
(D) Hughes later became president and rewrote the history
items.explanation: The review credits Hughes with the conference's dramatic move — stunning delegates by offering to scrap American ships under construction — making him the diplomat who shaped the outcome.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The scrapping proposal that defined the conference was Hughes's initiative.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Harding's administration convened the conference; the president did not oppose it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Treaties require Senate consent; the Secretary of State has no such sole power.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Hughes never became president; he later served as Chief Justice.
