items.stem: The review judges the Good Neighbor Policy a success: U.S.–Latin American relations were better on the eve of World War II than they had been in decades. What best explains the improvement?
options: (A) The United States increased its military occupations in the region
(B) Ending the occupations removed the main source of resentment
(C) Latin American nations adopted the Roosevelt Corollary themselves
(D) The Great Depression ended in 1933
items.explanation: Resentment had been caused by the occupations and the claimed right to intervene; removing both removed the grievance, which is why relations improved.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The occupations were wound down, not increased.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Non-intervention took away what Latin Americans had resented.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Corollary was the American claim Latin America opposed; no one adopted it.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Depression continued through the 1930s; the improvement came from the policy change.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Good Neighbor Policy (1930s) — it worked: U.S.-Latin American relations were better on the eve of World War II than they had been in decades

items.stem: The Nye Committee concluded that arms makers and bankers had dragged America into World War I. What did Congress conclude from this finding?
options: (A) The United States should join the League of Nations
(B) The arms makers should be put in charge of foreign policy
(C) The United States should declare war earlier in the next European conflict
(D) Economic ties caused the entanglement, so law must cut those ties
items.explanation: If business ties caused the war entry, the remedy was legal separation: the Neutrality Acts embargoed arms and banned loans to belligerents.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The finding pushed Congress toward neutrality laws, not toward the League.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Committee blamed the arms makers; Congress did not reward them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The entire point was to avoid the next war, not to enter it sooner.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The diagnosis (economic entanglement) dictated the prescription (legal bans on arms and loans).

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — Congress passed a series of Neutrality Acts driven by the Nye Committee's finding that arms makers and bankers had dragged America into World War I

items.stem: The review argues the Neutrality Acts rested on a misreading of 1917: German submarines, not economic ties, had caused the American war declaration. What follows from this judgment?
options: (A) The Nye Committee's premise was correct after all
(B) Submarines played no role in the First World War
(C) Economic ties were the true cause of the 1917 war declaration
(D) The laws attacked the wrong cause
items.explanation: If unrestricted submarine warfare caused the declaration, then cutting off arms sales and loans — the Neutrality Acts' remedy — attacked a cause that had not decided the matter.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review explicitly calls the premise a misreading.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The review says submarines were the cause; they plainly played a role.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. This restates the Nye premise the review rejects.
option_explanations.D: Correct. A remedy aimed at the wrong cause cannot prevent the outcome.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — the legislation rested on a misreading of 1917: economic ties hadn't caused the war declaration; German submarines had

items.stem: The 1937 Neutrality Act let belligerents buy non-military goods only if they paid cash and carried the goods away in their own ships. Though written impartially, why did "cash-and-carry" help Britain and France?

stimulus.text: The 1937 act added "cash-and-carry," letting belligerents buy non-military goods only if they paid cash and carried them in their own ships.

options: (A) British and French sea power meant only they could carry goods away
(B) They were the only countries in the world holding any cash reserves
(C) The act named Britain and France as its preferred buyers
(D) Germany possessed no merchant ships of its own at all
items.explanation: Impartial rules applied to unequal powers produce unequal results: the sea-lane advantage meant cash-and-carry was usable by Britain and France but not by Germany.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Control of the seas decided who could actually use the provision.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Many countries held cash; the constraint was carrying the goods, not paying for them.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The act was written to treat all belligerents alike; it named no favorites.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Germany had merchant shipping; the problem was getting it past British and French naval control.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — cash-and-carry in practice helped Britain and France, which controlled the sea lanes; neutrality failed because impartiality favors the strong

items.stem: Roosevelt chipped away at the Neutrality Acts — repealing the arms embargo in 1939 and winning Lend-Lease in 1941 — and Pearl Harbor ended the experiment. What does this arc from 1935 to 1941 show?
options: (A) American isolationism grew steadily stronger through 1941
(B) The isolationist peak receded as war neared
(C) Roosevelt remained a lifelong supporter of the Neutrality Acts throughout
(D) Pearl Harbor had no effect whatsoever on the neutrality laws
items.explanation: The sequence runs from the Acts' passage to their erosion to their end: the isolationist peak passed as the world crisis deepened, carrying America toward its postwar global role.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The repeal and Lend-Lease show isolationism weakening, not strengthening.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The arc is the bridge the review describes between 1930s neutrality and post-1941 globalism.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Roosevelt worked to undo the Acts, not to preserve them.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Pearl Harbor ended the neutrality experiment outright.

items.fact_source: u7.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Neutrality Acts (1935–37) — Roosevelt chipped away at the laws (repealing the arms embargo in 1939, Lend-Lease in 1941), and Pearl Harbor ended the experiment; the isolationist impulse's high-water mark, and the bridge between the 1930s and America's post-1941 globalism

items.stem: This 1846 daguerreotype shows Ralph Waldo Emerson, whose 1841 essay "Self-Reliance" declared: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string." According to the transcendentalists, where does truth come from?

stimulus.image_caption: Daguerreotype of Ralph Waldo Emerson, 1846.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1846 daguerreotype; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) From the doctrine of the church alone
(B) From the great philosophers of Europe alone
(C) From self-trust and nature, not institutions
(D) From the laws passed by the government
items.explanation: Emerson's creed, as the review summarizes it, located truth in the individual: self-trust and direct experience of nature outranked churches, parties, and inherited tradition.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The transcendentalists held that institutions, including churches, corrupted the individual.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Emerson urged Americans to stop imitating Europe, not to follow its philosophers.
option_explanations.C: Correct. "Trust thyself" is the doctrine: the individual, not the institution, is the source of truth.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Government law was among the institutions the transcendentalists distrusted.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — truth came from self-trust and direct experience of nature rather than tradition; Emerson's 1841 essay "Self-Reliance": "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string"

items.stem: This 1856 daguerreotype shows Henry David Thoreau. After spending a night in jail for refusing a poll tax during the Mexican War, he argued that conscience outranks law — an argument later abolitionists and civil-rights activists cited. What does that later citation show?

stimulus.image_caption: Daguerreotype of Henry David Thoreau, 1856.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1856 daguerreotype by Benjamin D. Maxham; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Thoreau personally led the later civil-rights movement
(B) The Mexican War ended because of his essay
(C) Poll taxes were abolished in 1849
(D) His principle outlived its moment and served later causes
items.explanation: An 1849 argument about a poll tax was still being cited a century later: the idea proved portable across reform movements and generations.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Thoreau died in 1862; later activists cited his writing, he did not lead them.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The war ended for military and diplomatic reasons, not because of the essay.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Poll taxes persisted long after 1849.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The citation history shows the principle's long afterlife in American reform.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — his 1849 essay on civil disobedience, written after he spent a night in jail for refusing a poll tax during the Mexican War, argued that conscience outranks law, a principle later abolitionists and civil-rights activists would cite

items.stem: The review stresses that transcendentalism "never was" a mass movement. A student concludes the movement was therefore historically unimportant. What is the best evaluation?
options: (A) Ideas matter more than membership: the circle fueled three reform movements
(B) The student is right, since only mass movements have ever mattered in all of history
(C) Transcendentalism actually counted millions of members
(D) Emerson and his circle actively opposed all of the reform movements
items.explanation: The review's whole point is that influence and membership are different measures: a small circle's ideas — individual self-trust applied to reform — powered causes far larger than the circle itself.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The movement matters as the intellectual fuel of the reform era, not as a mass organization.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Ideas from small groups have repeatedly shaped mass movements.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The review explicitly says it never was a mass movement.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The circle's confidence in individual remaking powered the era's reforms.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — transcendentalism matters for the exam not as a mass movement, it never was one, but as the intellectual fuel of the reform era; the same confidence that the individual could remake himself powered temperance, abolitionism, and women's rights

items.stem: This 1846 daguerreotype shows Margaret Fuller, a member of Emerson's circle. Her Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845) fed the Seneca Falls generation. What does this link show?

stimulus.image_caption: Daguerreotype of Margaret Fuller, 1846.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1846 daguerreotype by John Plumbe, Jr.; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Fuller personally organized the Seneca Falls convention
(B) Transcendentalist ideas fed the women's rights movement
(C) Emerson personally opposed the cause of women's rights
(D) Fuller's book was published after Seneca Falls met
items.explanation: Fuller's book carried the circle's confidence in individual self-remaking into the argument for women's rights, feeding the generation that met at Seneca Falls in 1848.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review says her book fed the Seneca Falls generation; Stanton and Mott organized the convention.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The link shows ideas traveling from the transcendentalist circle into women's rights.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Fuller was in Emerson's circle; nothing in the review suggests his opposition.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The book appeared in 1845, three years before Seneca Falls.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — Emerson's circle included Margaret Fuller, whose 1845 Woman in the Nineteenth Century fed the Seneca Falls generation

items.stem: Thomas Cole's The Oxbow (1836) shows the Connecticut River valley in sweeping detail. The review says such paintings taught viewers to see American nature as grander and purer than Europe's. What work were these paintings doing?

stimulus.image_caption: Thomas Cole, The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm), 1836 (Metropolitan Museum of Art).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1836 painting; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Highly detailed scientific surveys of American river systems
(B) Sustained criticism of westward expansion
(C) Political work: American nature as morally superior to Europe's
(D) Paid advertisements encouraging wealthy Europeans to tour America
items.explanation: The landscapes taught a political lesson alongside the aesthetic one: America's scenery proved the nation's providential assignment, which is why the review links the art to Manifest Destiny.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The paintings were art with a nationalist message, not scientific surveys.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The paintings celebrated the continent expansionists wanted, rather than criticizing expansion.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Grandeur on canvas became an argument for America's special destiny.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The intended audience was American, and the message was nationalist, not touristic.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Hudson River School — these landscapes taught viewers to see American nature as morally superior to Europe's: grander, purer, providentially assigned to Americans; that vision linked art to Manifest Destiny

items.stem: Cole's five-part series The Course of Empire (1833–36) warned that empires, like republics, could fall; its Destruction panel shows a civilization in ruins. What tension does this reveal in Cole's work?

stimulus.image_caption: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1836 painting; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) He opposed all forms of landscape painting
(B) He openly supported the great European empires of his own day
(C) He believed that the American republic could never fall
(D) Celebration and elegy for a wilderness he feared would vanish
items.explanation: The review reads Cole as both celebrant and mourner: the wilderness paintings glorify what he worried would disappear, and the Empire series warned republics could share Rome's fate.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Cole founded the landscape movement; he did not oppose it.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The series warns against imperial fate; it does not endorse empires.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The warning that republics could fall is the series' explicit theme.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The paintings are celebration shadowed by the fear of loss.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Hudson River School — The Oxbow (1836) and the five-part Course of Empire (1833–36), which warned that empires, like republics, could fall; Cole himself worried the wilderness would vanish, making the paintings both celebration and elegy

items.stem: Frederic Edwin Church's enormous canvases, like The Heart of the Andes shown here, toured American cities "like blockbusters." What does that touring show?

stimulus.image_caption: Frederic Edwin Church, The Heart of the Andes, 1859.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1859 painting; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Landscape art reached a wide audience beyond the elites
(B) Only the wealthy ever saw the paintings
(C) The paintings were deeply unpopular with the public
(D) The touring proved that Americans preferred European art
items.explanation: Blockbuster-style touring meant thousands of ordinary city-dwellers saw the canvases: the nationalist landscape message reached a mass public, not just collectors.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The touring model made the art a popular event, spreading its nationalist vision widely.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The blockbuster tours were designed for large public audiences.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The tours succeeded because the public flocked to them.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The appeal was precisely that the subjects were American, not European.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Hudson River School — Frederic Edwin Church carried the style west, painting on enormous canvases that toured cities like blockbusters

items.stem: Albert Bierstadt carried the Hudson River style west, painting the Rockies and Sierra Nevada on huge canvases just as expansionists were selling the West as a promised land. A student says these paintings were merely decorative. What is the best evaluation?

stimulus.image_caption: Albert Bierstadt, Rocky Mountain Landscape, 1870.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1870 painting; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Timing and subject show the paintings served expansion politics
(B) The student is right; none of the art of this era had political content
(C) Bierstadt personally opposed westward expansion
(D) The paintings were painted in Europe for European viewers
items.explanation: Paintings that arrive exactly when expansionists need a promised land, showing that land as grand and pure, are doing political work whether or not the painter carried a party card.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Subject, timing, and audience together make the nationalist argument.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The review explicitly says the paintings "did political work."
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. His western subjects served the expansionist vision, not opposition to it.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The paintings were made for American audiences as American subjects.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Hudson River School — Albert Bierstadt carried the style west; at a moment when expansionists were selling the West as a promised land, these landscapes taught viewers to see American nature as morally superior to Europe's; the paintings did political work

items.stem: The review says the transcendentalists were protesting a society that measured people by their output. What does this show about the Market Revolution era?
options: (A) Everyone living in the era celebrated the Market Revolution
(B) Transcendentalists supported factory discipline
(C) Critics saw human costs in the new market society
(D) The Market Revolution had no cultural effects at all
items.explanation: The Market Revolution's cultural cost is the review's phrase: in an age of factories and cash wages, the transcendentalists protested reducing persons to productivity.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The transcendentalists' protest shows celebration was not universal.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. They protested the output-measuring society; they did not support it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Economic transformation produced cultural criticism alongside economic nationalism.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The transcendentalist protest was itself a cultural effect of the Market Revolution.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — the movement also shows the Market Revolution's cultural cost: in an age of factories and cash wages, the transcendentalists were protesting a society that measured people by their output

items.stem: The Second Great Awakening was a mass revival that pushed Americans toward outward reform; transcendentalism was a small circle of New England intellectuals that turned the reforming impulse inward. What best distinguishes the two movements?
options: (A) They were the same movement operating under two different names
(B) The Awakening opposed all reform efforts
(C) Transcendentalism was the larger of the two
(D) A mass outward revival versus a small circle's inward turn
items.explanation: The review draws the contrast on both axes: the Awakening's mass, outward-moving revival energy against the transcendentalists' small, inward-turning circle.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review treats them as distinct: one mass and outward, the other small and inward.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Awakening pushed Americans toward reform; it did not oppose it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The review stresses transcendentalism never was a mass movement.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Scale (mass vs. circle) and direction (outward reform vs. inward self-culture) are the differences.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 Transcendentalism — as the Second Great Awakening pushed Americans toward reform, a smaller circle of New England intellectuals turned the reforming impulse inward

items.stem: This portrait shows Washington Irving, whose Sketch Book (1819–20) — with "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow" — proved American stories could sell, and be pirated, on both sides of the Atlantic. What does the piracy detail show?

stimulus.image_caption: Portrait of Washington Irving.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 19th-century portrait attributed to Charles Robert Leslie; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Americans could not read English
(B) Real transatlantic demand existed for American writing
(C) British authors outsold Irving in the American market
(D) Piracy ended American publishing
items.explanation: Pirates only steal what sells: the unauthorized editions on both sides of the Atlantic prove American stories had found paying audiences.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The demand for the books shows Americans were reading them.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Piracy is evidence of commercial demand, and it crossed the Atlantic.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The point is that an American author competed successfully, not that Britons outsold him.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. American publishing grew; piracy marked demand, not the industry's end.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 American literature finds a voice — Washington Irving's Sketch Book (1819–20), with "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow," proved American stories could sell, and be pirated, on both sides of the Atlantic

items.stem: This portrait shows James Fenimore Cooper. His Leatherstocking novels made the frontier — and the "vanishing Indian" in the era's romantic stereotype — the first distinctively American literary subject. What does the stereotype detail show?

stimulus.image_caption: James Fenimore Cooper, portrait by John Wesley Jarvis, 1822.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1822 portrait by John Wesley Jarvis; pre-1930 work, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Cooper opposed every racial stereotype of his era
(B) The Native peoples themselves wrote the Leatherstocking novels
(C) The frontier was not a real place
(D) American literature carried the era's racial assumptions
items.explanation: The "first distinctively American literary subject" came wrapped in the romantic "vanishing Indian" stereotype: national literature and racial assumption grew together.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The novels used the romantic stereotype; they did not oppose it.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Cooper, a white New Yorker, wrote the novels.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The frontier was real; the point is how literature depicted its peoples.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Celebrated national culture reproduced the era's racial ideas.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 American literature finds a voice — James Fenimore Cooper's Leatherstocking novels made the frontier, and the vanishing Indian in the era's romantic stereotype, the first distinctively American literary subject

items.stem: In his 1837 Phi Beta Kappa address "The American Scholar," Emerson called for an intellectual Declaration of Independence, urging Americans to stop imitating Europe. What was he calling for?

stimulus.text: In his 1837 Phi Beta Kappa address "The American Scholar," Emerson called for an intellectual Declaration of Independence, urging Americans to stop imitating Europe.

options: (A) A second war of independence against Britain
(B) The abolition of American colleges
(C) An American intellectual life independent of European models
(D) The imitation of French literature instead of British literature
items.explanation: The "intellectual" qualifier is everything: Emerson wanted cultural and intellectual independence — American thought on American terms — not another war.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The declaration he wanted was intellectual, not military.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. He addressed a college audience to reform its thinking, not to abolish it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Stop imitating Europe and think as Americans: that is the address's demand.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Swapping one European model for another is the opposite of his point.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 American literature finds a voice — in his 1837 Phi Beta Kappa address "The American Scholar," Emerson called for an intellectual Declaration of Independence, urging Americans to stop imitating Europe

items.stem: The review calls literary nationalism the "cultural twin" of the era's political and economic nationalism — the Monroe Doctrine abroad, the Market Revolution at home, and now a literature insisting American experience deserved its own voice. What pattern does this describe?
options: (A) The culture of the era actively opposed political nationalism
(B) The Monroe Doctrine was actually a work of literature
(C) The Market Revolution was purely cultural
(D) Nationalism ran through politics, economics, and culture
items.explanation: "Twin" means the same impulse in a second domain: the nationalism visible in Monroe's doctrine and in market expansion also appeared in books, paintings, and essays.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Culture reinforced nationalism; it did not oppose it.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The Monroe Doctrine was foreign policy; the point is the parallel, not identity.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Market Revolution was economic transformation with cultural effects.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The pattern is nationalism as a whole-era phenomenon across all three domains.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 American literature finds a voice — this literary nationalism was the cultural twin of the era's political and economic nationalism: Monroe Doctrine abroad, Market Revolution at home

items.stem: In 1800 American bookshelves were stocked with British authors; by the 1850s that had changed, and the review calls Irving and Cooper the first generation of professional American writers. What does "professional" imply here?
options: (A) They earned a living by writing for an American market
(B) They were paid salaries by the British government
(C) They wrote only about European subjects
(D) They soon abandoned writing for more respectable careers
items.explanation: "Professional" means the writing paid: by mid-century enough Americans bought American books to support full-time authors, a change from 1800's British-dominated shelves.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Professional status is evidence of a paying domestic readership.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Their market was American readers, not British patronage.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Their breakthrough was American subjects — the frontier, American stories.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. "Professional" means they stayed with writing as a career.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 American literature finds a voice — in 1800, American bookshelves were stocked with British authors; by the 1850s, that had changed; the first generation of professional American writers won domestic audiences

items.stem: The review concludes that post-War-of-1812 Americans, deciding what "American" meant, found their answer in the landscape itself. What does this show about culture's role in the era?
options: (A) Only politics and economics defined the nation; culture was irrelevant
(B) Culture did nation-building work alongside canals and elections
(C) The American landscape played no part in national identity
(D) Europeans decided what "American" meant
items.explanation: The review's closing argument is that nationalism ran through culture as well as politics and economics: paintings and books were instruments for deciding what "American" meant.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review's point is precisely that culture mattered as much as politics and economics.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Canals tied the country physically; art and literature tied it imaginatively.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The landscape was the answer, in the review's account, to the identity question.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The era's project was independence from European models, not deference to them.

items.fact_source: u4.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Hudson River School — Americans weren't just building canals and voting for Jackson; they were deciding what "American" meant, and the answer was the landscape itself

items.stem: The photograph shows the burial of Lakota dead at Wounded Knee, South Dakota, in the winter of 1890–91. The review calls Wounded Knee the conventional endpoint of the Indian wars. What does this scene of mass burial support?

stimulus.image_caption: Burial of the dead at the battle of Wounded Knee, South Dakota, winter of 1890–91 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1891 photograph, Library of Congress; published before 1930, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) The Lakota won the engagement
(B) The American soldiers suffered the heavier losses
(C) Some 250–300 Lakota dead, many women and children
(D) The mass burial took place before any shooting occurred
items.explanation: A mass burial is evidence of mass killing: the review's figures — some 250 to 300 Lakota dead, many women and children — match what the photograph shows.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The dead being buried are Lakota; the Army did the killing.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Army losses were small; the mass grave holds Lakota dead.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The image corroborates the scale and the civilian character of the killing.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The burial followed the December 29, 1890 shooting.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee (1890) — the soldiers opened up with rifles and Hotchkiss guns, killing roughly 250–300 Lakota, many of them women and children; Wounded Knee is the conventional endpoint of the Indian wars

items.stem: In 1889 the Northern Paiute holy man Wovoka preached that righteous living and the Ghost Dance would bring back the dead and the buffalo, and make whites disappear. The dance spread across the Plains "like fire." What kind of resistance was the Ghost Dance?
options: (A) A military alliance preparing to fight the U.S. Army
(B) A plan to abandon the reservations for Canada
(C) A demand for immediate U.S. citizenship
(D) Spiritual resistance: a religious movement of last hope
items.explanation: The review is explicit: the Ghost Dance was spiritual resistance — a vision of renewal through righteous living and dance — and agents who read it as a war dance misread it.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The review stresses it was not a war plan; the "war dance" reading was the settlers' fearful misreading.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The vision was about renewal on the Plains, not migration.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Citizenship came through the Dawes Act's allotment scheme, not through the Ghost Dance.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Dance, righteousness, and vision — the movement's weapons were spiritual.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee (1890) — Wovoka preached a vision of renewal: if Indians lived righteously and performed the Ghost Dance, the dead would return, the buffalo would come back, and whites would disappear; the Ghost Dance spread like fire as spiritual resistance, not a war plan, but a last hope

items.stem: This 1885 photograph shows Sitting Bull. In December 1890, reservation police tried to arrest him and killed him in the attempt; days later came the killing at Wounded Knee. What connects the two events?

stimulus.image_caption: Sitting Bull, photographed by D. F. Barry, 1885.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1885 photograph by D. F. Barry; published before 1930, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Sitting Bull personally led the Ghost Dance movement himself
(B) The same cavalry unit committed both of the killings
(C) Sitting Bull was killed at Wounded Knee itself in December
(D) Fearful misreading of the Ghost Dance as a war dance drove both
items.explanation: Terrified agents and settlers misread the spiritual movement as a coming war; that fear produced both the attempt to arrest Sitting Bull and the military confrontation at Wounded Knee days later.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The movement came from Wovoka, the Northern Paiute holy man, not from Sitting Bull.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Reservation police killed Sitting Bull; the Seventh Cavalry killed at Wounded Knee.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Sitting Bull died in the December arrest attempt, before and apart from Wounded Knee.
option_explanations.D: Correct. One misreading — Ghost Dance as war dance — drove both tragedies.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee (1890) — terrified agents and settlers misread it as a war dance; in December 1890, reservation police tried to arrest the Lakota leader Sitting Bull and killed him in the attempt; days later, on December 29, 1890, the Seventh Cavalry surrounded Big Foot's band at Wounded Knee Creek

items.stem: This photograph shows Big Foot (Si Tanka). On December 29, 1890, the Seventh Cavalry surrounded his band of Minneconjou Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota. What were the soldiers doing when the shooting started?

stimulus.image_caption: Big Foot (Si Tanka), chief of the Minneconjou Lakota.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 19th-century photograph; published before 1930, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) Disarming the band
(B) Signing a treaty with Big Foot
(C) Distributing food rations
(D) Building a fort at the creek
items.explanation: The shooting began during the disarmament of Big Foot's band; the review notes accounts differ on who fired first, but the context — a surrounded band being disarmed — is not in dispute.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The soldiers were in the middle of disarming the band when a shot was fired.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. No treaty council was underway; this was a military disarmament.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Rations had been cut reservation-wide, but the soldiers' task that day was disarmament.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The cavalry surrounded the band; it did not build a fort.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee (1890) — the Seventh Cavalry surrounded Big Foot's band of Minneconjou Lakota at Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota; during the disarmament a shot was fired, accounts differ on who fired first

items.stem: The review notes that accounts differ on who fired the first shot at Wounded Knee. What is the sound historical use of this uncertainty?
options: (A) It proves no Lakota people were killed
(B) It proves the soldiers acted in legitimate self-defense
(C) It limits first-shot claims; the one-sided outcome defines the event
(D) It means that historians can know nothing at all about Wounded Knee
items.explanation: Uncertainty about the first shot constrains one narrow claim; it does not erase the documented asymmetry of the killing that followed, which is the historically significant fact.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The mass burial and the review's figures establish the killing beyond doubt.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Uncertainty about the first shot does not establish the soldiers' justification.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Good history narrows claims to fit the evidence and weighs what the evidence does establish.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Much is documented — the surrounding, the weapons, the death toll; only the first shot is disputed.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee (1890) — during the disarmament a shot was fired, accounts differ on who fired first, and the soldiers opened up with rifles and Hotchkiss guns, killing roughly 250–300 Lakota, many of them women and children

items.stem: At Wounded Knee the soldiers opened up with rifles and Hotchkiss guns, killing roughly 250–300 Lakota, many of them women and children. What does the weaponry and the casualty pattern show?
options: (A) The Lakota were the better-armed side
(B) The Hotchkiss guns jammed and proved useless
(C) Very few people died in the engagement
(D) A one-sided slaughter rather than a battle
items.explanation: Artillery-class weapons fired into a band being disarmed, with women and children among the hundreds dead, describes a massacre, not a battle.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The band was being disarmed; the Army brought the heavy weapons.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The guns worked, which is why the death toll was so high.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Roughly 250–300 Lakota were killed.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The asymmetry of weapons and victims is the defining fact.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee (1890) — the soldiers opened up with rifles and Hotchkiss guns, killing roughly 250–300 Lakota, many of them women and children

items.stem: This photograph shows the Wounded Knee battleground. The review calls Wounded Knee the conventional endpoint of the Indian wars, adding that organized Native military resistance to the United States effectively ended there. A student claims Native resistance to U.S. power ended entirely in 1890. What is the best evaluation?

stimulus.image_caption: The battleground at Wounded Knee, South Dakota (Library of Congress photograph).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1890s photograph, Library of Congress; published before 1930, Public domain per Wikimedia Commons license tag

options: (A) The student is correct; all resistance ended in 1890
(B) The Indian wars continued as large-scale battles for decades afterwards
(C) Wounded Knee never actually happened
(D) Organized military resistance ended, leaving room for other forms
items.explanation: The review's wording is careful — "organized Native military resistance" — and the student's claim drops the qualifier, turning a precise endpoint into an overbroad one.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The claim ignores the qualifier and overstates what ended.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. No large-scale battles followed; the Indian wars as military campaigns ended.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The event is thoroughly documented.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Precision about what ended — organized military resistance — is what makes the endpoint claim defensible.

items.stem: The Dawes Act broke reservations into individual allotments of 160 acres per head of household, held in federal trust for 25 years, declared recipients U.S. citizens, and sold the "surplus" land to white settlers. What was the theory behind this design?
options: (A) The reservations would be enlarged and strengthened by law
(B) Private property would create farmers and dissolve tribalism
(C) Tribal governments would gain new powers
(D) Native peoples would be removed to Canada instead
items.explanation: The review names the assimilationist logic: individual ownership was supposed to manufacture yeoman farmers, and yeoman farmers would no longer need tribes.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The Act broke reservations up; it did not enlarge them.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Private property as a machine for assimilation was the theory.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. Dissolving tribalism was the goal, not empowering tribal governments.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The policy was allotment in place, not removal.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Dawes Act (1887) — intent vs. outcome — the theory being that private property would turn Indians into self-sufficient farmers; intended to dissolve tribalism by making Indians into yeoman farmers

items.stem: Under the Dawes Act, Indian-held land fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million by 1934. Reformers had celebrated allotment as liberation. What do the acreage figures do to the reformers' claim?
options: (A) They support the reformers' claim
(B) They are quite irrelevant to evaluating the policy's effects
(C) They refute it: two-thirds of the remaining land was lost
(D) They show that Indians gained land under allotment
items.explanation: The review's verdict rests on the numbers: a policy celebrated as liberation presided over the loss of about two-thirds of the land base, which is why the review says the acreage figures tell the real story.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Losing two-thirds of the land contradicts the liberation claim.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. Land loss is the central measure of an allotment policy's effects.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The figures convert the reformers' rhetoric into a testable — and failed — claim.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The figures show a fall from 138 million to 48 million acres.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Dawes Act (1887) — intent vs. outcome — Indians lost roughly two-thirds of their remaining land, from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million by 1934; reformers celebrated allotment as liberation; the acreage figures tell the real story

items.stem: Dawes allotments were too small and dry for Plains agriculture, much of the best land was declared surplus and sold outright, and the reservation map was checkerboarded with white ownership. How did these outcomes create the conditions for Wovoka's Ghost Dance?
options: (A) They made the Lakota wealthy enough to fund the movement itself
(B) They ended the reservation system entirely
(C) They brought the buffalo back to the Plains
(D) They produced poverty and desperation, in which renewal took hold
items.explanation: The review draws the causal chain directly: allotment produced poverty and dependence, and that desperation was the soil in which Wovoka's vision of renewal grew.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. Allotment produced poverty, not wealth.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The reservation system continued, checkerboarded and diminished.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The buffalo were gone; their return was the Ghost Dance's hoped-for vision, not its precondition.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Material desperation explains why a spiritual message of renewal spread like fire.

items.fact_source: u6.md §Added 2026-10-01 The Dawes Act (1887) — intent vs. outcome — allotment instead produced poverty and dependence, and created the desperation in which Wovoka's Ghost Dance took hold

items.stem: This American cartoon of 1798, titled "Property protected — à la Françoise," satirized French treatment of American property and diplomats. What American reaction to the XYZ Affair does it reflect?

options: (A) Federalist outrage at France and support for a hard line
(B) Support for a military alliance with France
(C) Indifference toward foreign affairs
(D) Democratic-Republican sympathy for the French position
items.explanation: The cartoon's mockery of French "protection" is Federalist in temper: anger at French insults to American diplomats and property, feeding support for the Quasi-War posture.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Satirizing France expressed the Federalist anger that the XYZ revelations produced.
option_explanations.B: Incorrect. The cartoon attacks France; it does not seek alliance with it.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. A biting political cartoon is evidence of engagement, not indifference.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. Democratic-Republicans were the pro-French faction; this cartoon's temper is Federalist.

items.stem: This portrait shows President John Adams. Under Adams, the XYZ Affair and the undeclared Quasi-War fed the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798, which criminalized criticism of the government; Jefferson and Madison answered with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions. What does this sequence show?

options: (A) Foreign policy had no domestic political effects
(B) A foreign crisis became a domestic fight over dissent and states' rights
(C) The Alien and Sedition Acts expanded freedom of speech
(D) Kentucky and Virginia supported the Federalist crackdown on dissent
items.explanation: A diplomatic crisis with France was converted into a domestic weapon — criminalizing criticism — which then provoked the states'-rights counterargument of nullification and interposition.

option_explanations.A: Incorrect. The sequence is precisely a foreign crisis reshaping domestic politics.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Each step — crisis, crackdown, constitutional counterargument — moved the fight from foreign to domestic ground.
option_explanations.C: Incorrect. The Acts criminalized criticism of the government; they restricted speech.
option_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions opposed the Acts with states'-rights doctrine.
